title: From Activity to Evidence
summary: Learn the difference between doing an activity, producing a work sample, creating an evidence candidate, and having evidence reviewed before stronger skill or competency claims can be made.
objectives: Distinguish activity, work product, evidence candidate, reviewed evidence, and competency decision.
Explain why completing an activity does not automatically prove a skill.
Identify what information helps connect evidence to the work that produced it.

vocab.def: A task, lesson, project, simulation, practice exercise, or other action a learner performs.
A work product or record that may be considered for review but is not automatically verified evidence.
Information showing where evidence came from, who created it, and the activity or source connected to it.
An authorized determination about whether evidence supports a defined competency.

sections.heading: Doing something and proving something are different
sections.body: Completing a lesson, project, simulation, or activity shows that an activity occurred. It does not automatically prove mastery, competency, professional qualification, or job readiness.

sections.heading: Work products can become evidence candidates
sections.body: A document, project, recording, design, analysis, presentation, or other work product can provide useful information about what a learner did. Before review, it should be treated as a candidate rather than verified proof.

sections.heading: Provenance connects the work to its source
sections.body: Useful evidence should make it possible to understand where the work came from, who produced it, what activity or project it belongs to, and which version or submission is being considered.

sections.heading: Review creates a stronger basis for a claim
sections.body: A stronger skill or competency claim may require authorized review against defined expectations. The learner can create the work, but the learner does not create their own institutional verification decision.

practice.prompt: A learner completes a project and uploads a final document. Does the upload automatically prove competency?
practice.answer: No. The document may be an evidence candidate, but competency requires the appropriate review and decision process.

practice.prompt: Why is it useful to know which project, submission, or version an artifact came from?
practice.answer: That provenance helps reviewers understand the source of the evidence and prevents unrelated or changed work from being mistaken for the reviewed source.

quiz.question: Which statement is most accurate?
options: A completed activity can produce an evidence candidate, but stronger claims may require review
Every completed lesson automatically proves mastery
A learner can mark their own competency as verified
Any uploaded file automatically becomes institutional evidence
quiz.answer: A completed activity can produce an evidence candidate, but stronger claims may require review

lab.objective: Review simulated learner activities and classify each item as an activity record, work product, evidence candidate, reviewed evidence, or competency decision.

reflectionPrompt: Why is it important to separate the fact that you completed an activity from the claim that you have proved a skill?
